newsitem.title: USA: TWA seen viable despite audit qualification.
newsitem.headline: TWA seen viable despite audit qualification.

text.p: Trans World Airlines Inc, whose auditor plans to qualify the carrier's 1996 results, faces no immediate risk of a bankruptcy filing, airline industry analysts said on Wednesday.

"Based on what we know today, I don't see TWA filing for bankruptcy anytime within the next six months," William Wrightson, an analyst at Alex Brown, said. "The real question is how the cash flow situation will look in six months."
TWA on Tuesday said its auditor, KPMG Peat Marwick LLP, would include a qualification on the airline's ability to continue as a going concern.

TWA spokesman John McDonald said the carrier still had confidence in its current business plan. "There has been much speculation since the announcement. KPMG said the same thing in 1994 and we're still here," he said.
McDonald said TWA was obliged to make the disclosure because of its plans to sell $50 million of senior secured notes.

They include the explosion and crash of Flight 800 off Long Island, New York, last July 17, the departure of chief executive officer Jeffrey Erickson and a call by union machinists for the resignation of acting CEO Gerald Gitner, who subsequently became chairman of the company.
In addition, Standard & Poor's Corp last week revised its ratings outlook on the airline to negative from developing.
The credit rating agency cited TWA's operating difficulties, reflected in a wider-than-expected fourth-quarter net loss of $170 million before special charges.
Stephen Klein, an analyst at S&P Equity Group, said TWA's plan to raise $50 million in a private placement should not be discounted when considering the carrier's future.
"It must be remembered here that auditors are not forward looking in terms of their approach, while analysts are looking at a lot of factors that are hard to quantify," Klein said.
"The company is not in trouble as far as a possible bankruptcy filing for this year, but only time will tell," he added.
Klein said it would take about six to nine months before it was clear whether a turnaround at TWA was indeed under way.
Glenn Engel, an analyst at Goldman Sachs, said the auditor's qualification was not a surprise, considering TWA's cash flow situation. Still, it could have a wider effect, he said.
"No one knows how it will affect bookings," Engel said. "But the publicity certainly doesn't help TWA."
